title: LBX1 alters polyamine pathway in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis – a new therapeutic target to mitigate curve progression

sections.abstract:
Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is the most common three-dimensional (3D) spinal deformity occurring during puberty, with girls at a higher risk of curve progression to the surgical threshold. Ladybird homeobox 1 (LBX1) is the most promising AIS predisposing gene based on GWAS studies, but its role in curve progression remains elusive.

The role of LBX1 in muscle phenotype and curve progression was investigated in clinical samples and mouse models. Additionally, metabolomic analysis was used to explore signaling pathway and potential therapeutic target.

In this study, we found elevated LBX1 and myogenic genes expression, along with increased proportion of type I muscle fibers, in the convex paraspinal muscle (PSM) of AIS patients. Notably, the concave/convex LBX1 ratio in PSM negatively correlates with curve severity. Using a 3D-printed asymmetric hypokyphosing thoracic restrainer, we established AIS-like 3D spinal deformities in young female mice, consistently inducing a thoracic right curve. AAV-mediated Lbx1 knockdown in concave PSM of Lbx1 fl/fl mice exacerbated curve progression by 50%. Mechanistically, Lbx1 knockdown inhibited myogenesis and muscle regeneration, and altered polyamine synthesis pathway. Key polyamine pathway enzymes ODC1 and SAT1 were reduced in concave PSM of AIS patients. The resultant lower serum level of spermidine, a key polyamine metabolite, was found in progressive AIS patients at their initial clinical visits. Importantly, daily spermidine supplementation significantly mitigated curve progression in scoliosis-like mice.

Our findings provide new evidence that differential Lbx1 expression in bilateral PSM exacerbates curve progression. The associated altered polyamine pathway and reduced circulating spermidine level represent novel therapeutic target and prognostic biomarker, respectively.

This study presents a straightforward and reproducible protocol for establishing a mouse model of spinal deformity with consistent curvature pattern for AIS research, and illustrates the potential role of the LBX1-mediated polyamine pathway in driving curve progression in AIS, which can be ameliorated by oral spermidine administration. Our findings highlight the modulation of paraspinal muscles as a viable approach to halting curve progression.

Keywords: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, Animal model, LBX1, Paraspinal muscle, Polyamine pathway, Translational research
sections.introduction:
Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a three-dimensional spinal deformity occurring predominantly in adolescent girls, with a prevalence of 1-4% worldwide [ 1 ]. Screening for AIS has received increasing attention in recent years, as untreated deformities may progress, particularly in patients who are still undergoing skeletal growth [ 2 , 3 ]. Due to unclear etiology and pathogenesis, current available treatments target anatomical changes instead of the causes. Bracing is the only evidence based non-surgical treatment for AIS, but about 25% of curves still progress beyond the surgical threshold [ 4 ]. Given that individuals with AIS often present with spinal curvature at their initial clinical visit, it is clinically more critical to understand the causes underlying curve progression severe curvature to develop personalized treatment regimen.

LBX1 is so far most promising AIS predisposing gene based on genome-wide association studies (GWAS) [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] ]. Differentiate expression of LBX1 in concave and convex paraspinal muscles has been reported in AIS, but the effects of such asymmetry on AIS was undetermined [ 9 , 10 ]. In mouse, Lbx1 is responsible for encoding a homeobox transcription factor that plays a role in the migration of muscle cells as well as the development of the cardiac and neural tube. Guo et al. reported that overexpression of human LBX1 in one-cell-stage embryos of zebrafish causes body curvature [ 11 ], although this more resembles congenital scoliosis. Matsuhashi et al. reported that global abrogation of Lbx1 in mouse skeletal muscle did not result in scoliosis [ 12 ]. On the other hand, patients with AIS appear to have weaker limb muscles strength than age and sex matched healthy subjects. It was reported that adolescents with higher lean mass at 10 years of age have a 20% lower scoliosis risk at 15 years of age [ 13 ]. Genetic analysis on multi-generation families, trios and sporadic AIS patients has identified a predisposing variants SLC6A9 encoding glycine transporter 1 which might lead to an increased plasma glycine level [ 14 ]. Furthermore, dysregulated galactose and glycolytic metabolism have been observed in progressive AIS, coinciding with the effect of LBX1 in human myoblast cells [ 9 ]. Collectively, these observations suggest that aberrant carbohydrate or other metabolic pathways during the adolescent growth spurt may disrupt growth trajectories, impair spinal stability, and thereby contribute to AIS onset and progression.

In human, the normal spine exhibits a slight pre-rotation in the horizontal plane, and its rotational pattern aligns with the direction commonly observed in the most prevalent types of scoliotic curves [ 15 , 16 ]. In the search for mechanism underlying curve progression of AIS, zebrafish is the most widely used animal model due to their susceptibility of lateral spinal deformity. The interspecies differences between human and zebrafish in terms of the force driving cerebrospinal fluid flow and the mechanisms controlling vertebral patterning suggests the need to develop mammalian model exhibiting rotational spinal deformity to address the knowledge gap [ [17] , [18] , [19] ]. Although surgical procedures, such as bipedal ambulation, unilateral resection of transverse processes, facet joints, ribs and spinal ligaments, and surgical damage of spinal cord have been proposed to induce experimental scoliosis models [ 20 , 21 ], the demanding surgical technique, questionable similarity to human AIS and ethical concerns have limited their applicability.

In this study, 4-week-old female mice were used to mimic the rapid skeletal growth phase and thus the higher risk of curve progression in spinal deformity. Referencing the dorsal-ventral and medial-lateral spinal deformities characteristic of right thoracic AIS patients [ [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] ], we designed a novel 3D-printed spinal restrainer to induce hypokyphosis and asymmetric loading, thereby compromising vertebral rotational stability and promoting progressive deformity in quadrupeds. Collectively, we hypothesized that this new mouse model enables the investigation of how differential LBX1 expression between concave and convex paraspinal muscles (PSM) could alter metabolism in PSM, thus increasing the risk of curve progression.
sections.methods:
28 Chinese AIS subjects with severe curvature and requiring posterior spinal surgery and instrumentation were recruited from Prince of Wales Hospital (CREC Ref. No. 2016.337), Nanjing Drum tower Hospital (2019-066-01) and the First Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University (2021-KYLL-39). Posterior paraspinal muscles of the concave and convex sides of apex of the major curve were collected intra-operatively. Subjects with other types of scoliosis with known causes or endocrine and connective tissue abnormalities were excluded as previously reported [ 26 ]. Freshly collected paraspinal muscles were immediately snap frozen in liquid nitrogen for RNA and protein, and embedded in OCT for histology and immunostaining. The basic information for the participants is presented in Supplementary Table 1 .

In this retrospective study, Chinese AIS girls between 10.0 and 13.5 years old at first visit with maximal Cobb angle <30° referred to our scoliosis special clinic between 2016 and 2019 were selected (CREC Ref. No. 2016.337). Cobb angle of major curve was measured from standard standing posterior-anterior radiography of the whole spine. Radiological Cobb angle was assessed at the first visit and at every 6 months interval until skeletal maturity. For AIS subjects with curve progression increased less than 6° according to Scoliosis Research Society criteria in the follow-up period were defined as nonprogressive group; while those progressed more than 6° and reached surgical threshold (>40°) at any time point within the 6-year follow-up were defined as progressive (P) group. 27 AIS subjects, whole blood samples were collected then aliquoted to minimize freeze-thaw cycle and stored at −80 °C for further analysis. The basic information for the participants was presented in Supplementary Table 2 . Informed consent was obtained before surgery and blood taking from all subjects or their guardians.

Owing to the higher prevalence of AIS in female adolescents, female and skeletally immature C57BL/6 and Lbx1-floxed mice (B6J-Lbx1em1Cflox/Nju) at the age of 4 weeks were used in this study. Mice were kept under pathogen free and 12 h light/dark cycle conditions with free access to food and water. We established a Lbx1 flox/flox mice strain with the exon 2 of mouse Lbx1 floxed by loxP sites via CRISPR/Cas9 system, thus the floxed exon 2 which encodes the functional homeodomin could be conditionally knocked out once CRE protein presents.

The whole asymmetric thoracic restrainer consisted of 2 parts. Both dorsal and ventral parts of the asymmetric thoracic restrainer was 17 mm long, 5 mm high, and 38.83 mm wide. The center of right and left side of dorsal part was 1 mm more dorsal or more ventral respectively. The ventral part was designed with a slope. The edges of the asymmetric thoracic restrainer were shaped in a semicircle or a ¼ circle for more space, and with 3 holes on extension for suturing to avoid dislocation. The asymmetric thoracic restrainer (2 g with a 1 mm thick wall) was printed with transparent resin VeroUltraTM WhiteS (RGD824) ( Fig. 2 A–C).

Generation of a novel mouse model of structural spinal deformity with consistent curve type. (A-C) Specifications of the 3D-printed restrainer used in the study. (D) Gross and X-ray images of 4-week-old female C57BL/6 mice subjected to the restrainer. (E) Representative X-ray images comparing control and model mice from 5 to 10 weeks of age. (F) Cobb angle measurements of control and model mice from 5 to 10 weeks of age. n = 10/group. (G) Representative micro-CT images of control and model mice at 10 weeks of age. Bar = 5 mm. (H) Analysis of AVT, ATR, and KI in control and model mice at 10 weeks of age. n = 5-7/group. (I) Representative images showing MyHC staining in control, concave, and convex sides of the PSM of the model at 10 weeks of age. bar = 100 um. (J) Muscle fiber type counting analysis of control, concave, and convex sides of PSM in the model at 10 weeks of age. n = 6-7/group. Result is shown with mean ± SD. Two-way ANOVA and Turkey post hoc (F), two-tailed t test (H), and One-way ANOVA and Turkey post hoc (J). ∗, p < 0.05, and ∗∗∗, p < 0.001.

4-week-old female mice were anesthetized by an intraperitoneal injection of ketamine (0.01 mg/g) and xylazine (0.005 mg/g). Then, the asymmetric thoracic restrainers were put on the mice and secured with 3-0 nylon sutures. All mice were kept under a 12-h dark-light cycle at constant room temperature, with food and water provided. All procedures were approved by the corresponding Animal Experimentation Ethics Committees. .

Please refer to Supplementary methods for further information.

Measurements of histological, X-ray and microCT results were performed by two blinded researchers. Two-tailed t test, paired t test, one-way or two-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc were used where appropriate. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. The data was presented in graphs as the mean and the standard deviation of the mean. SPSS software (Version 26.0) was used for above statistical analysis.
sections.results:
To compare the PSM phenotypes on the concave and convex sides and to investigate the association between LBX1 and PSM phenotypes, myogenic markers expression level and curvature, we collected bilateral PSM tissues at apical level from individuals with right thoracic AIS ( Supplementary Table 1 ). Analysis of muscle fiber type composition and cross-sectional area (CSA) showed significant differential type I muscle fibers in bilateral PSM. The proportion and CSA of type I fibers were markedly reduced in the concave PSM ( Fig. 1 A–C). Moreover, the expression of myogenic markers, including PAX7 , ACTA1 , ACTN2 , MYF6 , MYOD , and MYOG , is found significantly down-regulated in the concave PSM ( Fig. 1 D and F). Additionally, significant lower mRNA and protein levels of LBX1 is found in the concave PSM with paired samples from the same patient ( Fig. 1 E and F).

Asymmetrical paraspinal muscle (PSM) phenotypes and LBX1 expression in the concave and convex sides of PSM at the apex level in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). (A) Representative images showing myosin heavy chain (MHC) staining of PSM on the concave and convex sides. Scale bar = 250 um. (B, C) Percentage distribution of muscle fiber types and cross-sectional area (CSA) measurements in bilateral PSM of AIS subjects. n = 12/group. (D, E) Transcriptional levels of myogenic markers and LBX1 gene expression in bilateral PSM of AIS. n = 25-28/group. (F) Protein levels of myogenic markers and LBX1 in bilateral PSM of AIS. n = 3/group. (G) Correlation analysis between LBX1 and ACTA1 , ACTN2 , MYOD , MYOG , PAX7 and MYF6 in PSM of patients with AIS. n = 51-56. (H) Correlation analysis between transcriptional levels of LBX1 and Cobb angle in AIS. n = 28. Result is shown with mean ± SD. Two-tailed t test (B, C and D), paired t test (E) and Spearman's correlation. ∗, p < 0.05.

We next explored the correlation between LBX1 and myogenic markers expression levels in PSM of subjects with AIS. LBX1 expression was positively correlated with transcriptional levels of PAX7 , ACTA1 , ACTN2 , MYF6 , MYOD , and MYOG (p < 0.05) ( Fig. 1 G), suggesting the potential interaction between LBX1 and myogenesis in the bilateral PSM in AIS. Further correlation analysis demonstrated that the concave/convex LBX1 expression ratio was negatively correlated with maximal Cobb angle (p < 0.05), while LBX1 expression on either side alone was not significantly correlated with the maximal Cobb angle ( Fig. 1 H).

All mice could move around freely for food and water with restrainer on in the primary research center. Immediate sternum and spine rotation to the same direction was observed in all of the mice treated with the restrainer ( Fig. 2 D). All mice with the restrainer showed progressive right thoracic scoliosis phenotype, while all control mice did not show spinal deformity throughout the study period ( Fig. 2 E). The Cobb angle of the model increased weekly (p < 0.01) and finally reached to 30.8 ± 1.8° at 10-week-old, while controls remained stable ( Fig. 2 F). The body weight of the model increased steadily from 14.0 ± 0.7 g to 20.6 ± 1 g within the 6-week period. No significant body weight difference was detected between the model and control mice at each time point (p ≥ 0.05) ( Supplementary Fig. 2 ). To determine whether it is a structural curve, the asymmetric thoracic restrainer was removed at 10 weeks old after 6 weeks of restrainer treatment. Then, the whole-spine radiographs of the mice were monitored weekly for another 4 weeks ( Supplementary Fig. 3A ). The Cobb angle remained stable at 28.9 ± 2.9°, 28.8 ± 2.2°, 30.9 ± 2.4°, and 29.2 ± 2.3° at 11-, 12- 13- and 14-week-old, which is comparable to the Cobb angle of 29.9 ± 8.0° right before restrainer removal (p ≥ 0.05) ( Supplementary Fig. 3B ). The CT images at 4 weeks after removing the asymmetric thoracic restrainer ascertained the existence of the rotational curvature ( Supplementary Fig. 3C ). In the validation study, all mice with restrainers were able to move freely to access food and water. All treated mice developed a progressive right thoracic scoliosis phenotype, consistent with findings from the primary research center ( Supplementary Fig. 4A ). The Cobb angle in the model reached 35.4 ± 3.0° and 37.9 ± 3.1° in the two validation research centers, respectively, which were comparable to the results from the primary center ( Supplementary Fig. 4B ).

The monitoring of the 3D deformities characteristics was done via micro-CT imaging. Micro-CT imaging on 10-week-old model mice demonstrated a right thoracic-scoliosis like deformity on the coronal plane, vertebra rotation to the convex side at the apex level on transverse plane and hypokyphosis on the sagittal plane, indicating the establishment of a 3D spinal deformity model. The micro-CT images of untreated mice were also shown for composition ( Fig. 2 G). To quantify these deformities, the AVR, ATR and KI were measured and compared between the mice with and without the restrainer. The AVR, ATR and KI of the model were larger compared to that of the control mice, measuring up to 3.6 ± 0.7° (p < 0.05), 11.8 ± 1.1° (p < 0.05), 8.6 ± 0.8 (p < 0.05) at 7 weeks old, and 4.8 ± 0.7° (p < 0.05), 20.7 ± 1.6° (p < 0.05), 10.4 ± 1.5 (p < 0.05) at 10 weeks old respectively ( Fig. 2 H).

For muscle fiber type analysis, the concave and convex PSM at apical level from the mice treated with restrainer were compared with the right PSM harvested at the same vertebral level from the untreated mice. Type I muscle fiber composition was significantly lower at the concave-side PSM but significantly higher at convex-side PSM from the mice treated with the restrainer (p < 0.01). The convex-side PSM from the mice treated with the restrainer demonstrated a significant increase in type IIB muscle fiber composition (p < 0.01) ( Fig. 2 I and J). We also performed qPCR analysis of key myogenic regulatory factors (Myog and Myod) in bilateral paraspinal muscles of mice at baseline (4 weeks of age) and after restrainer treatment (10 weeks of age, following 6 weeks of bracing). Our results showed no significant differences in Myog or Myod expression between the concave and convex sides at either time point ( Supplementary Fig. 5 ). These findings align with those observed in patients with AIS [ 27 , 28 ]. Additionally, previous studies have indicated an increased proportion of type IIA muscle fibers on the concave side of the PSM in AIS patients. However, in the current study, we found no significant difference in the proportion of type IIA muscle fibers between the concave and convex sides of the PSM, which contrasts with earlier reports in AIS patients [ 27 , 28 ]. Moreover, caution should be paid because humans do not appear to have type IIB fibers when analyzing the MyHC composition [ 29 , 30 ].

To determine whether restrainer-induced curvature influences Lbx1 expression, we quantified Lbx1 mRNA levels in the concave and convex paraspinal muscles at baseline (before restrainer treatment) and after 6 weeks of restrainer treatment. No significant difference in Lbx1 expression was observed between the two sides at both two timepoint ( Supplementary Fig. 5 ). To assess the effect of differential Lbx1 expression in bilateral PSM on curve progression, we knocked down Lbx1 by injecting AAV9-Cre virus into the concave side of PSM near the 10th thoracic vertebra level (the apical level in the mouse model of scoliosis at 10 weeks old) of Lbx1 floxed mice (thereafter Lbx1 KD mice). Efficient targeting and accumulation of AAV9 in the paraspinal muscles were confirmed by in vivo fluorescence imaging. Indocyanine green (ICG)-labeled AAV9 produced strong fluorescent signals exclusively on the injected (concave) side, whereas the contralateral non-injected side showed no detectable signal. Mice without injection or receiving PBS injection similarly exhibited no fluorescence ( Supplementary Fig. 6A–B ). Both Lbx1 KD mice and control mice were subsequently treated with or without restrainer and monitored using X-ray and micro-CT ( Fig. 3 A). Lbx1 mRNA expression remained significantly down-regulated at two- and six-weeks post injection ( Fig. 3 B). X-ray analysis showed that Lbx1 knockdown in one side of PSM alone did not induce spinal deformity in the absence of restrainer. The spine remained stable in both control and Lbx1 KD mice without restrainer, whereas restrained Lbx1 KD mice displayed significantly larger Cobb angle (41.5 ± 4.2°) when compared with that of restrained controls (27.8 ± 1.1°) ( Fig. 3 C and D). Micro-CT analysis corroborated these observations. In the absence of restrainer, neither group displayed evident spinal deformities. However, restrained Lbx1 KD mice exhibited significantly more pronounced 3D spinal deformities, including hypokyphosis, vertebral rotation, and trunk rotation, compared to restrained control mice ( Fig. 3 E). The KI, AVR, and ATR (12.4 ± 1.3 Vs 10.1 ± 1.6, 16.8 ± 1.6 Vs 8.5 ± 1.1°, and 29.1 ± 2.0 Vs 18.2 ± 1.3°, respectively) were all significantly higher in restrained Lbx1 KD mice than restrained control mice ( Fig. 3 F). Muscle fiber type analysis revealed that Lbx1 KD in the PSM was sufficient to decrease type I fiber content, regardless of restrainer, consistent with the reduced type I fiber phenotype observed in the concave PSM of AIS with lower LBX1 expression and in the concave PSM of a mouse model of spinal deformity induced by restrainer. Additionally, Lbx1 KD increased type IIB fiber content, mirroring the changes observed in wild-type mice subjected to restrainer ( Fig. 3 G and H). Collectively, these results indicate that asymmetric Lbx1 expression in bilateral PSM exacerbates scoliosis progression in the mouse model.

Down-regulation of Lbx1 in the concave side of the PSM exacerbated scoliosis progression in the mouse model. (A) Schematic illustration of AAV9-Cre virus application and detection of spinal deformities. (B) mRNA expression levels of Lbx1 in the concave side of the PSM in 4-week-old female C57BL/6 mice, assessed 2 and 6 weeks post-control or AAV9-Cre virus treatment. (C) Representative X-ray images of control and Lbx1 knockdown (KD) mice, with or without restrainer treatment, from 5 to 10 weeks of age. (D) Representative micro-CT images of control and Lbx1 KD mice, with or without restrainer treatment, at 10 weeks of age. Bar = 5 mm. (E) Cobb angle measurements in control and Lbx1 KD mice, with or without restrainer treatment, from 5 to 10 weeks of age. n = 5 -7/group. (F) KI, AVR, and ATR analyses in control and Lbx1 KD mice, with or without restrainer treatment, at 10 weeks of age. n = 5-7/group. (G) Representative MyHC images of the left (without restrainer) and concave side (with restrainer) PSM in control and Lbx1 KD mice at 10 weeks of age. Blue indicates type I fibers, green type IIA, red type IIB, and black type IIX. bar = 100 μm. (H) Muscle fiber type counting analysis of the left (without restrainer) and concave side (with restrainer) PSM in control and Lbx1 KD mice at 10 weeks of age. n = 4/group. Data are shown with mean ± SD. Two-tailed t test (B), One-way ANOVA and Turkey post hoc (D, F and H). ∗, p < 0.05.

We utilized a widely used muscle injury mouse model to explore the potential function of Lbx1 in muscle. After knocking down Lbx1, the gastrocnemius muscles were subjected to BaCl 2 injection and collected at different time points for assessment ( Fig. 4 A). H & E analysis showed the muscle regeneration process of both control and Lbx1 KD mice ( Fig. 4 B). Fourteen days post BaCl 2 injection, the CSA of gastrocnemius muscle fibers in Lbx1 KD mice were significantly smaller than that of controls, although the percentage of centrally nucleated fibers did not differ significantly ( Fig. 4 B and C). qPCR analysis revealed that myogenic markers, including Pax7 , Myod , Myog and Myf6 , were significantly downregulated in gastrocnemius muscle of Lbx1 KD mice ( Fig. 4 D). Western blot analysis further confirmed that Myod expression level was down-regulated in Lbx1 KD mice ( Fig. 4 E and F). To further illustrate the effect of Lbx1 on muscle repair process, we tested the mechanical function of the gastrocnemius muscles of Lbx1 KD and control mice 14 days after BaCl 2 injection. The force of gastrocnemius muscles in Lbx1 KD mice was reduced compared to that of control mice at different frequency ( Fig. 4 G). Additionally, the twitch force of gastrocnemius muscles in Lbx1 KD mice were significantly reduced, though the tetanic force was not differential significantly ( Fig. 4 H).

Lbx1 dysregulation impaired myogenic activities. (A) A schematic illustration of the Lbx1 knocking down and muscle injury. (B) H & E staining shows muscle repair process in gastrocnemius muscles at day 4, 6, 10 and 14 in control side and Lbx1-KD side. bar = 100 μm. (C) Cross-sectional area (CSA) and percentage of central nuclear fibers of gastrocnemius muscle 14 days after injury. n = 7/group. (D) Transcriptional level of Lbx1 and myogenic markers after injury in control side and lbx1 -KD side. n = 5/group. (E, F)Protein level of LBX1 and myogenic markers after injury in control side and Lbx1-KD side. n = 3/group. (G, H) Muscle functional test at day 14 in control side and Lbx1-KD side. n = 7/group. (I) mRNA level of LBX1 in LBX1 knocked down cells (KD) and in negative control cells at baseline (D0) and day four (D4). n = 3/time point. (J) mRNA expression level of myogenic markers in control cells and KD cells at D4. n = 3/group. (K) Myotube formation (MF20 positive staining) in control and KD cells after four days fusion. Scale bar = 250 μm. Result is shown with mean ± SD. Two-tailed t test. ∗, p < 0.05.

Furthermore, we explored the role of LBX1 in myogenic differentiation using human skeletal muscle myoblasts (HSMM) cells. qPCR analysis revealed that LBX1 expression was low at baseline (D0) but increased progressively during the myogenic fusion process (D0–D4) ( Fig. 4 I). LBX1 knockdown significantly led to reduced mRNA levels of myogenic markers including PAX7 , MYOG and MYF5 after four days of differentiation ( Fig. 4 J). Immunofluorescence staining showed that myotubes formation was apparently observable as indicated by positive staining of MF20 on day 4 of myogenic differentiation in wide type control HSMM cells. In contrast, there was no noticeable myotubes formation in the LBX1 KD HSMM cells ( Fig. 4 K). Collectively, these results demonstrate that LBX1 appears to modulate muscle regeneration and myogenesis.

Metabolomics analysis was conducted on control and LBX1-overexpressing (OE) cells (N = 3) ( Supplementary Fig. 7 ) to identify metabolic pathways influenced by LBX1 overexpression. To validate the findings, the experiment was independently repeated with a larger sample size (N = 6 for control and LBX1-OE cells). In both the initial and confirmatory experiments, four metabolites exhibited significantly reduced levels in LBX1-OE cells compared to control cells, while twenty-four metabolites showed significantly increased levels in LBX1-OE cells across both batches. The top two metabolites with the highest fold changes (FC) in the OPLS-DA model for LBX1-OE cells relative to control cells were putrescine (FC = 1.5 in batch 1, FC = 2.2 in batch 2) and spermine (FC = 1.5 in batch 1, FC = 1.8 in batch 2), both associated with the polyamine synthesis pathway [ 31 ]. Furthermore, two upstream metabolites in this pathway, arginine (FC = 1.4 in batch 1, FC = 1.6 in batch 2) and ornithine (FC = 1.5 in both batches), were also significantly elevated in LBX1-OE cells compared to control cells ( Fig. 5 A).

Polyamine synthesis pathway was altered with LBX1 dysregulation. (A) Metabolites with significantly differential levels in two batches of screening studies. Each column shows the metabolic pattern of individual cell in the first batch (n = 3) and second batch (n = 6). Metabolites with significant difference between LBX1 over-expressed (OE) Vs control HSMM cells in both batches are listed as relative value and is represented by the color scheme in which red and blue indicate high and low concentrations of metabolites, respectively. (B, C) Protein expression levels of LBX1, myogenic markers, and enzymes involved in the polyamine synthesis pathway in control and LBX1-OE HSMM cells. n = 3. (D) Transcriptional levels of polyamine synthesis enzymes in the gastrocnemius muscles of control and Lbx1 knockdown (KD) mice. n = 5/group. (E, F) Protein levels of polyamine synthesis enzymes in the gastrocnemius muscles of control and Lbx1 KD mice. n = 3/group. Result is shown with mean ± SD. Two-tailed t test. ∗, p < 0.05.

To confirm the role of the polyamine synthesis pathway in LBX1 dysregulation, we examined the expression of key enzymes in LBX1-OE HSMM cells. In LBX1-OE cells, both protein and mRNA levels of myogenic markers (MYOD, MYOG) and polyamine synthesis enzymes (ODC1, SAT1) were significantly upregulated compared to controls ( Fig. 5 B and C). Conversely, Lbx1 knockdown (KD) in mouse gastrocnemius muscles significantly reduced the mRNA and protein levels of Odc1 and Sat1 ( Fig. 5 D–F). These findings indicate a novel role for LBX1 in regulating the polyamine synthesis pathway in muscle tissue.

To assess whether the polyamine synthesis pathway was altered in the PSM of Lbx1 KD mice, we harvested apical PSM tissues from both control and Lbx1 KD mice, with and without restrainer treatment. Consistent with observations in gastrocnemius tissues ( Fig. 4 ), Lbx1 KD significantly down-regulated myogenic marker ( Myod ) in PSM, regardless of restrainer ( Fig. 6 A and B). Furthermore, protein levels of key polyamine synthesis enzymes, Odc1 and Sat1, were also significantly downregulated in Lbx1 KD PSM tissues ( Fig. 6 A and B). Notably, restrainer treatment itself had no effect on the expression of the myogenic marker or polyamine synthesis enzymes. To explore whether this pathway was similarly affected in AIS patients, we examined bilateral PSM tissues from clinical samples. Western blot analysis revealed significant downregulation of ODC1 and SAT1 in the concave side PSM compared to the convex side ( Fig. 6 C and D). These findings confirm that reduced Lbx1 and LBX1 expression leads to decreased expression of key polyamine synthesis enzymes in the PSM of both Lbx1 KD mice and AIS patients, respectively.

Alteration of polyamine synthesis pathway in paraspinal muscle of Lbx1 KD mice and AIS subjects. (A, B) Protein levels of Lbx1, Myod and polyamine synthesis enzymes in left (without restrainer) and concave side (with restrainer) PSM of control and Lbx1 KD mice at 10 weeks of age. n = 3/group. (C, D) Protein levels of polyamine synthesis enzymes in the apex level bilateral PSM of AIS subjects. n = 3/group. (E) Serum spermidine levels of non-progressive and progressive (Cobb angle ≤40° and Cobb angle >40°) AIS patients at the first visit (Cobb angle <30°). n = 10-15/group. Result is shown with mean ± SD. One-way ANOVA and Turkey post hoc (B, E), and two-tailed t test (D). ∗, p < 0.05.

Given that the polyamine synthesis pathway was altered in the PSM of AIS subjects, we further examined the association between serum spermidine level and risk of curve progression in AIS patients. Serum samples were collected at their first visit whose Cobb angle less than 30°. Patients were subsequently followed longitudinally and classified into non-progressive and progressive AIS groups. Progressive AIS was defined as a Cobb angle increase of >6° but remaining <40°, or a Cobb angle ≥40° during follow-up. Spermidine levels did not differ significantly between non-progressive and progressive AIS patients with Cobb angle less than 40°. However, patients with progressive AIS and Cobb angles more than 40° had significantly reduced serum spermidine levels ( Fig. 6 E). These results support that serum spermidine level was able to predict subsequent progression in AIS.

Based on the above evidence, reduced Lbx1 expression in the concave PSM may impair the polyamine synthesis pathway, leading to altered muscle fiber type proportions and contributing to curve progression in restrained Lbx1 KD mice. We hypothesized that supplementation with spermidine, a critical intermediate in the polyamine synthesis pathway essential for producing polyamines such as putrescine, spermidine, and spermine, could restore polyamine synthesis in the concave PSM and mitigate curve progression. To test this, restrained control and Lbx1 KD mice were treated with 3 mM spermidine or a vehicle control from 4 to 10 weeks of age ( Fig. 7 A). Spermidine supplementation significantly increased serum spermidine levels (15179.0 ± 3025.5 Vs 7514.7 ± 931.5 pg/mL, and 14723.6 ± 6053.7 Vs 7026.2 ± 1973.4 pg/mL in control and Lbx1 KD mice groups, respectively) in both groups without affecting body weight ( Fig. 7 B).

Dietary spermidine alleviated curve progression of Lbx1 KD mice in mouse model of scoliosis. (A) A schematic illustration of spermidine treatment and spinal deformity detection. (B) Plasma spermidine levels and bodyweight of mice treated with vehicle control and spermidine. n = 6-7/group. (C) Representative X-ray images of control and Lbx1 KD mice subjected to vehicle control or spermidine treatment. (D) Cobb angle measurements of control and Lbx1 KD mice subjected to vehicle control or spermidine treatment. n = 6-7/group. (E) Representative micro-CT images of control and Lbx1 KD mice with vehicle control or spermidine treatment at 10 weeks old. Bar = 5 mm. (F) KI, AVR and ATR analysis of control and Lbx1 KD mice with vehicle control or spermidine treatment at 10 weeks old. n = 5-7/group. (G) Representative MyHC images of concave side PSM in control and Lbx1 KD mice with vehicle control or spermidine treatment at 10 weeks old. Blue, type I. Green, type IIA. Red, type IIB. bar = 100 μm. (H) Muscle fiber type counting analysis of concave side PSM in control and Lbx1 KD mice with vehicle control or spermidine treatment at 10 weeks old. n = 4/group. (I, J) Protein levels of Myod in concave side PSM of control and Lbx1 KD mice with vehicle control or spermidine treatment at 10 weeks old. n = 3/group. Result is shown with mean ± SD. One-way ANOVA, Turkey post hoc. ∗, p < 0.05.

X-ray analysis showed that spermidine treatment had no effect on spinal deformity in control mice, with Cobb angles remaining comparable between the spermidine-treated and vehicle control groups at all time points ( Fig. 7 C). In contrast, spermidine treatment in restrained Lbx1 KD mice significantly reduced curve progression, resulting in a Cobb angle reduction of 6.2°compared to untreated restrained Lbx1 KD mice ( Fig. 7 D). Micro-CT analysis further validated these findings from a three-dimensional perspective ( Fig. 7 E). In control mice, spermidine did not affect kyphosis, vertebral rotation, or trunk rotation, with no significant differences in kyphotic index (KI), axial vertebral rotation (AVR), or axial trunk rotation (ATR) between the spermidine-treated and vehicle control groups ( Fig. 7 F). However, in Lbx1 KD mice, dietary spermidine alleviated hypokyphosis and significantly reduced vertebral and trunk rotation, leading to significant decreases in KI, AVR, and ATR by 1.2, 4.0°and 4.9°, respectively ( Fig. 7 F).

Histological analysis indicated that spermidine did not alter type I fiber counts in control mice but significantly mitigated the reduction of type I fiber counts in restrained Lbx1 KD mice ( Fig. 7 G and H). Similarly, spermidine had no effect on myod protein levels in control mice but restored myod expression in restrained Lbx1 KD mice ( Fig. 7 I and J). These results demonstrate that dietary spermidine effectively attenuates curve progression and three-dimensional spinal deformities in restrained Lbx1 KD mice by restoring polyamine synthesis and supporting muscle function.
sections.discussion:
In this study, the effect of LBX1 on curve progression was confirmed using a newly developed mouse model of scoliosis that exhibits 3D spinal deformity features similar to those observed in AIS patients. Metabolomics analyses uncovered a novel role for LBX1 in the polyamine synthesis pathway, which underlies the worsened curve progression in restrained mice with Lbx1 knockdown in their concave PSM - a process that can be alleviated through daily spermidine supplementation. Notably, this alteration in the polyamine pathway among AIS patients with severe curves may occur even during the initial stages of progression, as evidenced by markedly reduced circulating spermidine levels in progressive AIS individuals who presented with mild curves at their first clinical evaluation.

AIS typically affects individuals between the ages of 10 and 18 years old. This age range in humans corresponds to 4 to 12 weeks of age in mice, a period which they undergo rapid skeletal growth and are considered skeletally immature [ 32 , 33 ]. The selection of young mice with rapid skeletal growth and skeletal immaturity corresponds to human adolescents, making this model more clinically relevant. From animal welfare perspective, all the studied mice could move freely in the cage for food and water with restrainer on, and there was no negative effect on body weight, skin appearance and bone mass throughout the study period, implying good adaptability of the mice. AIS is a multifactorial disease. Despite the etiology and pathogenesis remain largely unclear, from mechanical perspective, it has been speculated that the pre-deformed spine exhibits a slight pre-rotation in the horizontal plane making it vulnerable to deformation, and its rotational pattern aligns with the direction commonly observed in the most prevalent types of scoliotic curves [ 15 , 16 ]. When the spine undergoes decompensation and develops scoliosis, the preexisting rotation further intensifies, adhering to the inherent pattern already established [ 34 ]. Thoracic hypokyphosis has been proposed as one of the factors facilitating vertebra rotation, thus promoting curve progression [ 34 , 35 ]. In our model, the external asymmetrical compression induces hypokyphosis and thoracic cavity rotation. While AIS develops spontaneously in humans without external compression, in this model, the restrainer was designed to induce hypokyphosis and asymmetric thoracic loading in skeletally rapid growing 4-week-old mice, compromising vertebral rotational stability in quadrupeds and leading to progressive structural deformity to mimic the proposed biomechanical distortion in AIS at early stage of onset and progression. The successful development of 3D spinal deformity in quadrupedal animals with relatively more spine stability further illustrates the critical role of rotatory decompensation and hypokyphosis on scoliosis progression. Of note, it has been speculated that the direction of the spinal rotational deformity determines the direction of the resulting scoliotic curve. Specifically, leftward vertebral rotations lead to left-sided scoliotic curves, while rightward rotations result in right-sided curves [ 15 , 16 ]. In current study, the asymmetric thoracic restrainer consistently imposes the desired direction of rotation to induce a predictable curve type. Collectively, this new model mimics spinal deformity in AIS, such as lateral spinal curvature, vertebral rotation on the transverse plane and hypokyphosis on the sagittal plan, as well as paraspinal muscle fiber types change. Its clinically relevant phenotypes, reproducibility and high successful rate (comparing with other scoliosis models with successful rate ranging from 50% to 80% [ 20 , [36] , [37] , [38] , [39] , [40] ]) make this newly developed scoliosis model a promising tool for studying the effects of candidate genes/metabolites on disease progression.

Regarding the differential expression of LBX1, William et al. reported a contradictory result that the levels of the LBX1 gene were not significantly different between concave and convex PSM of the scoliotic curve in a group of 25 AIS patients whose Cobb angles met the surgical correction criteria (mean Cobb angle 68.8° ± 15.4°) in a Caucasian population [ 41 ]. However, two previous studies, comprising cohorts of 24 and 134 patients respectively, have reported consistent findings with current study, wherein LBX1 expression was diminished on the concave side PSM in individuals with AIS [ 9 , 10 ]. Our group previously compared LBX1 expression in paraspinal muscles from AIS patients and age-matched non-AIS controls and found no significant difference between non-scoliotic muscle and either the convex or concave paraspinal muscles in AIS [ 9 ]. However, a clear expression asymmetry was present between the convex and concave sides within AIS patients, suggesting that this imbalance reflects an inherent feature of AIS rather than a global change in LBX1 expression. Notably, such asymmetry was not observed in patients with congenital scoliosis despite comparable curve severity, further supporting the notion that differential LBX1 expression in paraspinal muscle is specific to AIS [ 10 ]. Several mechanisms have been proposed to account for the asymmetric LBX1 expression observed in PSM of AIS. Genetic factors may contribute to this imbalance; for instance, the AIS-associated SNP rs1322330 reduces LBX1 promoter activity, resulting in lower overall LBX1 expression that is particularly pronounced on the concave side. This reduction has been associated with decreased myofiber size, lower proportion of type I fibers, and impaired myosatellite cell function [ 10 ]. Epigenetic mechanisms have also been implicated, with differential methylation of the LBX1 promoter reported between concave and convex sides in patients with severe curves, indicating potential local modulation of LBX1 transcription [ 42 ]. In addition, PAX3 acts as an upstream regulator of LBX1. In Pax3-deficient mice, Lbx1 expression is markedly reduced in somatic region [ 43 , 44 ], and PAX3 itself is downregulated in concave side PSM of AIS patients [ 45 ], suggesting that altered PAX3 signaling may drive the observed LBX1 asymmetry. Although mechanical stress represents an alternative explanation, Lbx1 mRNA levels showed no convex and concave difference in paraspinal muscles of our restrainer-induced scoliosis mouse model ( Supplementary Fig. 5 ), indicating that mechanical deformity alone is insufficient to induce this pattern. Collectively, these findings support the view that asymmetric LBX1 expression in AIS primarily arises from disease-specific genetic and epigenetic alterations rather than as a secondary consequence of spinal curvature.

The link between LBX1 and myogenic markers in AIS suggests a potential association between asymmetrically expressed LBX1 and imbalanced muscle phenotype of AIS. By using our new mouse model, we are able to demonstrate for the first time that differential Lbx1 expression in bilateral PSM can exacerbate curve progression, rather than inducing curve onset. We found that Lbx1 knockdown in mice has profound effect on reducing type I muscle fiber. Type I fiber is low twitch fiber, with more mitochondria and higher endurance [ 46 ]. Type I muscle fibers are known to generate lower tension compared to type II muscle fibers [ 47 , 48 ]. The decrease of type I fiber in concave PSM may lead to asymmetrical stress on the left and right side of the spine, and further exacerbate curve progression. This finding aligns with a previous study by Shao et al., which reported that decreased expression of the Estrogen Receptor 1 (ESR1) gene in the concave side PSM of a biped mouse model of scoliosis led to a smaller muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) and increased spinal curvature [ 49 ]. On top of these, we further show that such altered polyamine synthesis pathway occurs in AIS concave PSM whereas LBX1 expression is down-regulation. More importantly, progressive AIS subjects have lower serum spermidine level even at their first clinical visit, suggesting the altered polyamine synthesis pathway in AIS represents a novel prognostic biomarker for curve prediction in AIS.

Dysregulated polyamines have been associated with a range of muscular and skeletal disorders, including Snyder–Robinson syndrome (SRS) [ 50 ], amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) [ 51 ] and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) [ 52 ]. Our findings align with previous research on the polyamine synthesis pathway and its role in muscle function. Chiara et al. demonstrated that knockdown of Paox/Smox, key enzymes in the polyamine synthesis pathway, in Drosophila resulted in significant muscle dysfunction, as evidenced by increased fatigue in a top climbing assay [ 53 ]. Zhang et al. reported that intraperitoneal injection of 100 mg/kg spermidine in 8-week-old male C57BL/6 mice for 32 days activated satellite cells, although it was associated with side effects such as gastrocnemius muscle atrophy [ 54 ]. Additionally, Martina et al. found that spermidine improved muscle defects in COL6/collagen VI-related myopathies by reactivating autophagy in mice [ 55 , 56 ]. These studies, together with our results, indicate that alteration of the polyamine synthesis pathway contributes to muscle dysfunction, and spermidine supplementation can ameliorate impaired muscle phenotypes. However, further investigation is warranted to determine if LBX1 could modulate polyamine pathway through binding to the promotors of polyamine metabolism genes, such as ODC1 and SAT1. Previous studies have shown that spermidine functions as a regulatory metabolite that promotes satellite cell activation and muscle regeneration through the spermidine–eIF5A axis [ 57 ]. Given that impaired muscle regeneration has been proposed as a contributing factor and potential therapeutic target in AIS [ 58 ], this pathway may partly explain the beneficial effects observed in our model. The mitigating effect of spermidine on curve progression in our Lbx1 KD mouse model is particularly notable. From clinical perspective, early intervention with spermidine, when the Cobb angle is below 20°, could potentially reduce the need for bracing. Furthermore, combining spermidine supplementation with bracing for Cobb angles between 20 and 40° may lower the risk of progression to the surgical threshold. Importantly, spermidine treatment did not affect bone phenotype (data not shown), a known factor in curve progression, suggesting that its beneficial effects are primarily driven by improvements in muscle function. AAV-mediated LBX1 overexpression poses substantial safety concerns, including off-target effects, long-term gene expression, immunogenicity, and the challenges of delivering gene therapy to paraspinal muscles in adolescents. In contrast, spermidine, a natural polyamine present in various foods, has been investigated in several clinical trials involving adults, including older populations. These studies have explored oral spermidine supplementation at doses ranging from 0.9 to 3.3 mg per day over 3 to 12 months, reporting potential benefits for cognitive performance, inflammation, and verbal memory with minimal adverse events [ [59] , [60] , [61] , [62] , [63] , [64] ]. However, the safety and efficacy of spermidine supplementation in adolescents remain unstudied, necessitating further research to evaluate its potential benefits and risks in this population.

The current study has certain limitations. First, the results from our novel mouse model of scoliosis should be interpreted cautiously due to biomechanical differences between quadrupedal mice and bipedal humans. Quadrupedal models cannot replicate the unique posterior shear force inherent to human bipedalism, which predisposes the upright spine to rotational instability. Our study therefore focuses not on etiology of onset but of progression. We show that mechanical stress alone can initiate scoliosis in mice, while genetic susceptibility synergistically accelerates curve progression under the same mechanical insult. Thus, our findings highlight a critical gene-environment interaction driving deformity severity. Second, the exclusive use of female mice limits the generalizability of the findings, despite the higher susceptibility of female AIS patients to curve progression [ 65 ]. Future studies will include male cohorts to determine whether the LBX1–polyamine mechanism is sex specific. Moreover, although spermidine rescued the phenotype, its exact cellular mechanism in paraspinal muscle is unknown. We did not test processes such as autophagy, mitochondrial function, or specific signaling pathways. Future work is needed to clarify how spermidine acts. In conclusion, our study provides comprehensive preclinical and clinical evidence supporting a novel mechanism involving the LBX1-mediated polyamine synthesis pathway in the progression of three-dimensional spinal deformities. These findings warrant further investigation to explore its potential as a new therapeutic approach for AIS.
